summary:
Trend Detective is a web app that teaches to test claims such as "my town is getting drier" against NASA Earth-science data. The user picks a place and a variable (air temperature from MERRA-2, rainfall from GPM IMERG, soil moisture from GLDAS), predicts the answer, and then sees the result. The app removes the seasonal cycle, fits a trend, tests it with a method that corrects for autocorrelation, and gives a plain-language verdict: significant increase, significant decrease, or not enough evidence.

The core feature is the window explorer. It recomputes the trend for every start and end year, so the user sees how the conclusion changes with the period chosen. In the Po Valley, rainfall from 2013 to 2022 shows a significant drying trend, but 2001 to 2025 shows none. Same data, different conclusions.

This matters because cherry-picked time periods are behind many climate misunderstandings. Trend Detective does not tell users what is true. It shows them how to check.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Trend Detective is a web app that lets students test a claim such as "my town is getting drier" against NASA data. The user picks a place (seven presets in different climates, or any coordinates) and a variable: air temperature (MERRA-2), rainfall (GPM IMERG) or topsoil moisture (GLDAS). Before seeing any result, the user predicts the answer. The app then gives a plain-language verdict: significant increase, significant decrease, or not enough evidence.

HOW IT WORKS

1. The app downloads monthly series for one grid cell from the NASA GES DISC Giovanni time-series API and checks the units against a catalogue.

2. It removes the seasonal cycle by subtracting each calendar month's long-term mean.

3. It fits a linear trend and tests it with an OLS test whose standard error is corrected for autocorrelation. Missing months are never filled.

4. It cross-checks the result with a Newey-West test and a Sen slope, and shows a warning when the methods disagree.

5. It tests whether the finding survives other start years, neighbouring grid cells and stricter data-coverage rules.

6. It reports the smallest trend the record can detect, so "not enough evidence" is never read as "no change".

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most trend tools give one plot and one p-value. Our core feature is the window explorer. It recomputes the trend for every start and end year with at least 10 complete years of data, so the user sees how the conclusion depends on the period chosen. In the Po Valley, rainfall from 2013 to 2022 shows a significant drying trend, but 2001 to 2025 shows none. Of 135 possible windows, 19 are significant: 8 downward and 11 upward. Milan temperature is the opposite case: 416 of 666 windows are significant, and all of them point upward. The tool lets users tell a robust trend from a cherry-picked one. The predict-first step makes users confront their own expectations before they see the data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Claims about local climate change are everywhere, and many rest on a well-chosen start year. Trend Detective teaches high-school and college students, journalists and local decision-makers to ask the right question: does this finding survive a reasonable change of window, place or method? Our guiding idea: we don't tell you what's true; we show you how to check.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty over drama: a calibrated test, an explicit "not enough evidence" verdict, and warnings when methods disagree.

- We checked the false-positive rate by simulation. Our test gave 3.8% to 7.3% false positives on 1000 no-trend series per setting, against a 5% target. We dropped seasonal Mann-Kendall because it gave 22%. The script and seed are in the repository.

- Results describe one grid cell, not a city, and the app says so.

- Only real NASA data. If data cannot load, the app shows an error instead of synthetic values.

- We chose the preset places for climate diversity and data coverage before looking at any result.

TOOLS

Python 3.11, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, Plotly, pytest (offline test suite against cached data), the NASA Giovanni time-series API, and GitHub. SI use: Anthropic's Claude assisted with code and text; the README's "Use of AI" section gives the details. The app itself has no AI feature.
dataRefs: MERRA-2 monthly single-level diagnostics V5.12.4 (M2IMNXASM), 2 m air temperature
GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 monthly 0.1° V07 (GPM_3IMERGM)
GLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4 monthly 0.25° V2.1, soil moisture 0–10 cm
NASA GES DISC Giovanni in the Cloud: Time Series Service
projectRefs: Weatherhead et al. (1998), trend detection and years needed
Hirsch, Slack & Smith (1982), seasonal trend tests
Claude Code (Anthropic), SI coding and writing assistant
